bills.headline: Updates Georgia banking rules, adding new financial and oversight requirements for mortgage lenders and brokers.
bills.recap: This law updates many parts of Georgia's banking code. For mortgage companies, it sets minimum net worth and cash requirements: $50,000 for brokers, and $100,000 plus $1 million in liquidity for most lenders. Lenders must get a yearly outside audit, and both lenders and brokers must have a board of directors, a risk management program, and internal audits. It also tightens background checks, barring anyone with certain financial crimes like fraud or theft at any time, and it limits mailers that show a homeowner's loan details unless they clearly say they are not from the borrower's lender. Realtors may see small mortgage shops face higher costs or consolidate, which could affect the lenders they refer clients to.

bills.title: Healthy Food Access Tax Credit Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 2 of Chapter 7 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to imposition, rate, computation, exemption, and credits from income taxes, so as to provide for a tax credit for the construction, renovation, purchase, or lease of a property for taxpayers who place in service an eligible retailer that sells or offers for sale healthy foods in a less developed area; to provide for definitions; to provide for terms and conditions; to provide for rules and regulations; to provide a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

bills.headline: Creates a 15% state tax credit for building or leasing healthy food stores in underserved areas.
bills.recap: This bill creates a Georgia income tax credit equal to 15% of what a business spends to build, renovate, buy, or lease property for a store that sells fresh fruits and vegetables in a state-designated less developed area. Eligible stores include grocery stores, corner stores, convenience stores, farmers' markets, and small food retailers. The credit starts with tax years beginning January 1, 2026, can only be claimed in the year the store opens, and unused amounts can carry forward five years. Realtors who work in commercial leasing or sales may see more demand for retail space in these areas, since the credit can lower the cost of buying or leasing property there.

bills.headline: Creates a $10,000 Colquitt County homestead exemption, pending a 2026 local vote.
bills.recap: This law gives Colquitt County homeowners a $10,000 exemption off the assessed value of their home for county property taxes, covering up to five acres. versions.changes: First version of the bill.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Finance Committee rewrote the bill but kept its main goal: the surviving spouse (who has not remarried) or minor children of a qualifying disabled veteran can keep the homestead tax exemption on a future home, not just the original one. The new version defines "minor" as under 18 and ends a child's exemption at the end of the tax year the child turns 18. It also adds a rule that county tax assessors may ask exemption holders to prove they still qualify no more than once every three years, with no more than three doctors' letters. Finally, it updates the cross-references in the free license plate law and the vehicle tax exemption for disabled veterans, and it still requires a statewide vote in November 2026 before taking effect January 1, 2027.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: This new Senate Finance Committee version drops the section that would have changed the definition of "disabled veteran" for free license plates and the car tax exemption for disabled veterans. The main part of the bill stays the same: it lets the unremarried surviving spouse or minor children of a qualified disabled veteran keep the veteran's homestead property tax exemption. Voters would still decide in a statewide referendum in November 2026, and if approved it would take effect January 1, 2027. The other edits are only renumbering and formatting.

bills.headline: Lets surviving spouses and minor children of disabled veterans keep their tax exemption after moving.
bills.recap: Today, the unremarried surviving spouse or minor children of a qualified disabled veteran can keep the veteran's homestead tax exemption only on the home they already live in. This bill lets them carry the exemption to any future homestead they own and live in, as long as they file once in the new county. A child's exemption ends at the end of the tax year they turn 18, and tax assessors can ask for proof of eligibility no more than once every three years. It needs a two-thirds vote in both chambers and statewide voter approval in November 2026, taking effect January 1, 2027. For Realtors, it means these surviving families can sell and buy a new home without losing a major property tax break.

bills.title: Georgia HOA Accountability and Community Empowerment Act (HACEA); enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Articles 3 and 6 of Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to condominium associations and property owners' associations, respectively, so as to provide requirements for board members for condominium associations and property owners' associations; to provide for allocation of votes; to provide for proxies; to provide for quorums; to provide for residency for board members; to provide for size requirements for boards; to provide for board elections, filing, and certification; to provide for contests of election results; to provide for annual registration requirements for such associations; to provide for a short title; to provide for a purpose; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for severability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

bills.headline: Sets new election, voting, and board rules for Georgia condo associations and HOAs.
bills.recap: This bill gives each condo unit or HOA lot one vote and requires boards of at least three members who own and live in the community, with only one board member per home. Boards must be elected at least once a year, keep scanned ballots for owner review, and file election results with the Secretary of State, which would certify results, hear election challenges, and could suspend associations that don't meet the board-size rule. Annual meetings would count as having a quorum no matter how many owners attend. Realtors may care because the bill changes how communities are governed, could bar investor or out-of-town owners from serving on boards, and may affect buyers weighing HOA or condo properties.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 5C of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to title ad valorem tax on motor vehicles, so as to expand the definition of a rental motor vehicle with respect to the tax; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version drops the plan to add certain specially modified vehicles to the definition of a rental motor vehicle. Instead, it creates a split payment option for the title ad valorem tax (the one-time tax paid when titling a vehicle). For-hire charter buses or motor coaches (built for more than 15 passengers) and specially modified rental vehicles would pay 50 percent when applying for a title and the other 50 percent within 12 months. It also repeals an existing paragraph (7.1) of the law and slightly changes the modified vehicle rules so they cover renting to any business, not just "other" businesses.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: No meaningful changes were made to HB 66 in this version. The header now names the sponsors, Representatives Stephens and Fleming, instead of saying the House Ways and Means Committee offered the substitute, and some page spacing was cleaned up. The bill's wording on rental motor vehicles and property tax is the same as before.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Finance Committee turned this small vehicle-tax bill into a much bigger one. It adds a new optional 1 percent county sales tax, called the Alternative Homestead Option Sales and Use Tax, that voters must approve together with a local law creating an extra homestead exemption on county property taxes. Up to 25 percent of the money can go to capital projects (roads only for the county), and the rest pays for the homestead exemption, which can reach up to 100 percent of a home's assessed value. The tax and exemption end after ten years unless voters approve them again. The original vehicle provision stays: charter buses and certain specially modified rental vehicles can still pay half the title tax up front and the rest within 12 months, but owners of modified rental vehicles must now file an affidavit confirming they qualify.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The new Senate Finance substitute drops the motor vehicle section, so it no longer lets for-hire charter buses or certain specially modified rental vehicles pay half the title tax up front and the rest within 12 months. What remains is the optional county sales tax of 1 percent, approved by voters, that would fund a homestead exemption of up to 100 percent of a home's assessed value for county taxes, with some money also going to capital projects. Key dates moved forward one year: the short title is now the 2026 Act, and the cutoff for 'existing' versus 'qualified' cities is now January 1, 2027. Most other changes are minor wording and formatting fixes.

bills.headline: Lets counties adopt a 1% sales tax to fund bigger homestead property tax exemptions.
bills.recap: This Senate substitute replaces the bill's original rental car topic. It lets Georgia counties ask voters to approve a new 1% local sales tax, paired with a local act creating an extra homestead exemption that could cover up to 100% of a home's assessed value for county taxes. Up to 25% of the money can go to road projects and city capital projects. The rest must lower county taxes on primary homes, with any leftover used to roll back the county tax rate. Both the tax and the exemption must pass in the same vote, and they end after 10 years unless voters renew them. Realtors may care because lower property tax bills on primary homes can make owning more affordable and change carrying costs for buyers.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Ways and Means Committee's version keeps the main change: local governments get until May 1, 2025, instead of March 1, to opt out of the statewide base year homestead exemption. The new version adds a rule that the law takes effect as soon as the Governor signs it, or as soon as it becomes law without a signature. That matters because the new deadline is close. The rest is small wording cleanup, such as saying 'website' instead of 'public website' in the notice rules.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The new version greatly expands the bill. The deadline for cities, counties and school districts to opt out of the statewide base year homestead exemption moves to March 31, 2029, instead of May 1, 2025. An opt-out applies to a given tax year only if it is filed by March 31 of that year, and one of the three required public hearings must be held within 30 days before it takes effect. The bill also confirms that a surviving spouse does not need to reapply for the exemption. It adds new property tax notice rules: local governments must certify an estimated roll-back rate by March 31. Assessment notices must show that rate or an estimated tax amount, and tax bills must carry a bold warning when the adopted millage rate is higher than the estimated roll-back rate. The changes apply to tax years starting January 1, 2025.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Rules Committee version cuts the opt-out extension way back. Local governments now have only until March 31, 2025 to opt out of the statewide base year homestead exemption, not March 31, 2029 as the earlier Ways and Means version allowed. It also drops the rule that one public hearing be held within 30 days of the opt-out taking effect, and it removes the separate rule on which tax year an opt-out applies to. New in this version: a local government that already opted out can reverse that choice by passing a resolution and filing it with the Secretary of State by March 31, 2025.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The edits only touch formatting: the document code now starts with "25," the header names the Rules Committee substitute and lists sponsors such as Rep. Blackmon, and page footers were cleaned up. The bill's actual wording, including the March 31, 2025 opt-out deadline, is the same.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Finance version keeps the March 1, 2025 deadline for local governments to opt out of the statewide base year homestead exemption, instead of moving it to March 31. Any government that opted out must now redo the hearings and file a new resolution by March 1 every year for the opt-out to stay in effect after 2025. A government can cancel its opt-out at any time, and it takes effect for a tax year if filed by March 1 of that year. The version also spells out that the homestead covers the main home and up to five connected acres, or a narrower area for certain specially assessed land. It changes the assessment notice: it must show each local government's estimated rollback rate if certified at least 15 days before the notice is mailed, or the prior year's millage rate if not, and it drops the option to show an estimated tax bill.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Rules version drops the rule that local governments must repeat the opt-out steps every year. Instead, governments that opted out of the statewide homestead exemption from HB 581 (2024) and have no base-year exemption of their own must redo the hearings and refile by March 1, 2027. They can reverse an opt-out for 2025 by April 30, 2025, or for 2026 through 2029 by March 1 of that year. Through 2029, tax bills in those areas must also print a bold notice saying the local government opted out of homeowner tax relief, with a phone number to call. The bill now covers more ground: it refunds local sales taxes on building materials for school projects in systems that have a base-year homestead exemption (until 2033), adjusts local sales tax caps and the special district property-tax-relief sales tax, and adds an estimated tax amount to assessment notices when a roll-back rate is not certified.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed between the Senate committee version and the final enrolled version of HB 92. The only edits are formatting: new header labels showing the bill passed both the House and Senate, a list of sponsors, page labels, and one fixed typo. The bill's substance, including the rules on opting out of the base year homestead exemption, tax bill notices, and the local sales tax exemption for school construction materials, is the same.

bills.headline: Tweaks Georgia's homestead tax freeze, opt-out rules, tax bills, and assessment notices.
bills.recap: This new law updates the statewide base-year homestead exemption from HB 581 (2024), which limits how fast a home's taxable value can rise. Local governments that opted out must repeat public hearings and refile by March 1, 2027 to stay opted out, can reverse their opt-out through 2029, and must print a bold notice on homeowners' tax bills saying they opted out. Surviving spouses do not need to reapply. Assessment notices must now use a statewide form and show each local government's estimated roll-back rate, and tax bills must flag when the adopted rate is higher. Realtors can use this to explain property tax relief, and future tax bills, to buyers and sellers in different counties.

bills.recap: Georgia's conservation use program lowers property taxes on farm and timber land. Before, the land lost that break if it was leased to someone who could not qualify for it. This law lets owners lease to certain registered farm businesses and keep the break. The business must be owned only by U.S. citizens, focus on farming or timber, and earn at least 80% of its income from those uses in Georgia, or have a member who owns at least 25% of the leased land and qualifies. The bill also renews a film postproduction tax credit through 2030 and applies starting in tax year 2026. Agents who sell or list farm and timber land may want to know about the new leasing option.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Code Section 8-3-201 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, Article 1 of Chapter 1 of Title 20 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, Chapter 1 of Title 34 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, and Article 2 of Chapter 19 of Title 45 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to definitions relative to fair housing, general provisions regarding education, general provisions regarding labor and industrial relations, and fair employment practices, respectively, so as to prohibit discrimination based on hairstyles associated with race, color, or national origin; to provide for definitions; to provide for a civil cause of action; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

bills.headline: Adds hair texture and protective hairstyles to Georgia's fair housing definition of race.
bills.recap: This bill updates Georgia's Fair Housing Act so that 'race' includes traits like hair texture and protective hairstyles such as braids, locs, and twists. That means treating a buyer or renter differently because of their hairstyle could count as illegal race discrimination in housing. The bill also adds similar protections in schools and jobs, with a right to sue for workplace violations. Realtors, brokers, landlords, and property managers should know that hairstyle-based bias would be covered under state fair housing rules.

bills.recap: This law raises the limit on bonds and notes the Georgia Housing and Finance Authority (GHFA) can have outstanding for its single-family housing program, from $3 billion to $6 billion. These bonds help fund the state's home loan programs, such as Georgia Dream. A higher cap gives the state room to finance more mortgages for eligible buyers. Realtors working with first-time or moderate-income buyers may see these programs stay available longer. The law took effect when the Governor signed it.

versions.changes: The committee replaced the whole bill with a new one about the Georgia standard deduction. The original version would have ended a tax credit for businesses that buy or lease vehicles for employee transportation. It also would have dropped two sales tax breaks, one for film rentals and one for clean-room air equipment, and added a sales tax break for nonprofit affordable housing work. All of that is gone; the new version keeps the standard deduction at $24,000 for married couples filing jointly and $12,000 for other filers, lets taxpayers add certain federally defined net disaster losses on top of it, and applies to tax years starting January 1, 2024.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The only edits are to the header, which now lists the bill's sponsors (Representatives Franklin, Frye, Williams, Werkheiser, Cameron and others) instead of naming the House Ways and Means Committee, plus small spacing fixes. The bill's actual content, including the standard deduction amounts shown, is the same.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate Finance Committee replaced the whole bill with a new subject. The earlier version raised the state income tax standard deduction to $24,000 for married couples filing jointly and $12,000 for other filers. The new version instead changes the state sales tax break on manufactured homes: 50% of the sales price is exempt if the home is installed under state rules and converted to real property within 30 days of the retail sale, and the home must be a dwelling with an angled roof and at least 650 square feet. If the seller does not file the Certificate of Permanent Location in time, the state recovers 1.5 times the exempted tax; the home cannot go back to personal property unless the exempted tax is repaid; local sales taxes still apply; and the change takes effect July 1, 2026.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in the bill's content between the Senate committee version and the final enrolled version. The only edits are labels and headers: the document now shows it passed both the House and Senate and lists its sponsors, led by Representative Franklin. The rules on manufactured homes and the July 1, 2026 start date are the same.

bills.headline: Cuts state sales tax on manufactured homes converted to real property by half.
bills.recap: Starting July 1, 2026, this law exempts 50% of the sales price of a manufactured home from Georgia state sales tax. To qualify, the home must be properly installed and converted to real property within 30 days of the sale. It must also be a dwelling of at least 650 square feet with an angled roof. The seller must file a Certificate of Permanent Location with the clerk of superior court within 30 days, or pay 1.5 times the tax that was exempted. The home cannot later be turned back into personal property unless the exempted tax is repaid. Local sales taxes still apply. Realtors working with manufactured homes on land may see lower purchase costs for buyers.

bills.title: Criminal procedure; extend certain protections for victims of family violence and stalking with respect to residential leases
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 17, Title 19, and Title 44 of the O.C.G.A., relating to criminal procedure, domestic relations, and property, respectively, so as to extend certain protections for victims of family violence and stalking with respect to residential leases; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

bills.headline: Expands lease protections for family violence and stalking victims, including removing abusers from shared rentals.
bills.recap: This bill lets a tenant protected by a family violence or stalking order end their own lease on a shared rental with 30 days' written notice, without ending the lease for other tenants. It also lets the victim ask the landlord to end only the abuser's lease, with at least 72 hours' posted notice to the abuser. Landlords cannot raise rent, add deposits, or charge early termination fees to remaining tenants. Landlords also cannot refuse to rent to, refuse to renew, or evict someone for being a victim, or face a lawsuit. Property managers and leasing agents should know these rules apply to leases signed or renewed after the law takes effect and cannot be waived in the lease.

bills.title: Property; prohibit condominium and property owners' associations from retaliating against property owners for taking certain actions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to prohibit condominium associations and property owners' associations from retaliating against property owners for taking certain actions; to provide for circumstances that are not considered retaliation; to provide definitions; to provide for remedies; to provide for a defense; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

bills.headline: Bars condo and HOA boards from retaliating against owners who complain or assert rights.
bills.recap: This bill stops condo associations and property owners' associations from punishing owners who file complaints, give feedback, use their legal rights, or organize other owners. Banned retaliation includes raising an owner's fees, cutting services, blocking use of their home or common areas, or suddenly suing or filing to foreclose on a lien. If an owner raised a life, health, safety, or habitability concern and the association acted against them within three months, that counts as early proof of retaliation. Owners could use retaliation as a defense to a lien foreclosure and recover one month's fees plus $500, court costs, and attorney's fees, which matters for Realtors working with buyers and sellers in HOA and condo communities.

bills.title: Mortgage lenders and brokers; prohibit unfair or deceptive practices in consumer transactions related to mortgage trigger leads
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 2 of Article 15 of Chapter 1 of Title 10 and Article 13 of Chapter 1 of Title 7 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the Fair Business Practices Act and licensing of mortgage lenders and mortgage brokers, respectively, so as to prohibit unfair or deceptive practices in consumer transactions related to mortgage trigger leads; to provide for definitions; to provide for a remedy; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

bills.headline: Cracks down on deceptive mortgage solicitations using credit-check 'trigger leads' sold to other lenders.
bills.recap: When a buyer applies for a mortgage, the credit check can be sold as a 'trigger lead' to other lenders, who then call or mail the buyer with competing offers. This law makes it an unfair or deceptive practice for those lenders and brokers to hide that they are not tied to the buyer's original lender, skip making a firm offer of credit, contact people on the do-not-call list or who opted out of prescreened offers, or advertise rates and terms they know will change for the worse. Violations can be punished under Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act and are also grounds for action against a mortgage license. Realtors may care because it helps protect buyer clients from confusing or bait-and-switch calls during the loan process, which can reduce surprises before closing.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from City of Newnan ad valorem taxes for municipal purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the base year assessed value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.changes: First version of the bill.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House local legislation committee replaced the original bill with a substitute. The only real change sets the voter referendum on the Newnan homestead exemption for the November 2025 general election date. The original version said only "the Tuesday after the first Monday in November" with no year. The exemption itself, which limits taxable value increases on homesteads, is unchanged; the other edits are formatting and labels.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in the bill's content. This version only updates the header to list the bill's sponsors, Representatives Smith of the 70th and Bonner of the 73rd, in place of the committee's substitute note. There is also a small spacing fix in the title. The proposed Newnan homestead exemption itself is the same as before.

versions.changes: Nothing of substance changed between the committee version and the final enrolled version. The only edits are labels, showing the bill passed both the House and Senate. The Newnan homestead exemption, which works off a base-year value, and the local voter referendum are the same as in the committee version.

bills.headline: Freezes Newnan city property tax assessments on homesteads at base-year value, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill creates a City of Newnan homestead exemption that blocks city taxes on any rise in a home's assessed value above its base-year value. It covers up to five contiguous acres. New improvements or added land are still taxed, and city taxes for bond debt, county, school, and state taxes are not affected. Homeowners must apply once, and the exemption renews each year while they live there. The base year resets when a home sells, so buyers start fresh at the new value. The exemption needed approval from Newnan voters in November 2025 and would start January 1, 2026.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; increase amount of a state-wide homestead exemption from certain ad valorem taxes
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Part 1 of Article 2 of Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property tax exemptions, so as to increase the amount of a state-wide homestead exemption from certain ad valorem taxes; to provide for related matters; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, and automatic repeal; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

bills.headline: Raises Georgia's statewide homestead exemption from $2,000 to $5,000, pending voter approval.
bills.recap: This bill would raise the basic statewide homestead exemption from $2,000 to $5,000 of a home's value for owner-occupied primary residences. It applies to state, county, and school property taxes, but not to city taxes, city school taxes, or taxes used to pay off bonds. It needs a two-thirds vote in both chambers and approval by statewide voters by November 2026; if approved, it takes effect January 1, 2027. Realtors may care because it would modestly lower yearly property tax bills for homeowners, which can help with owning costs.

bills.title: Eviction Service and Airplane Evictions Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 7 of Chapter 10 of Title 9 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to continuances, so as to provide for the continuance and stay of proceedings related to eviction of tenants at certain airports; to provide for a definition; to amend Code Section 44-7-51 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to issuance of summons, service, time for answer, and defenses and counterclaims, so as to provide for service by an approved process server; to provide for related matters; to provide a short title; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee version drops the whole airport section. That section would have paused evictions of airport tenants, except for unpaid rent, while a federal aviation complaint was pending. The bill is renamed the "Eviction Service Act" and now only lets an approved process server, along with the sheriff or a constable, serve eviction papers. bills.headline: Lets approved process servers, not just sheriffs or constables, serve eviction papers.
bills.recap: This law, called the Eviction Service Act, changes who can deliver eviction court papers to tenants in Georgia. Before, only a sheriff, deputy, or county constable could serve the summons and affidavit. Now an approved process server can do it too, using the same rules for hand delivery, leaving papers with an adult at the home, or posting and mailing them. Landlords and property managers may see faster service and fewer delays in eviction cases.

bills.title: Courts; remote online notaries public and remote online notarizations; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 2 of Chapter 6 of Title 15 and Article 1 of Chapter 17 of Title 45 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to clerks of superior courts and general provisions regarding notaries public, respectively, so as to provide for remote online notaries public and remote online notarizations; to provide requirements for electronic journaling; to amend Part 2 of Article 15 of Chapter 1 of Title 10, Part 1 of Article 1 of Chapter 2 of Title 44 and Article 4 of Chapter 18 of Title 50 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to the "Fair Business Practices Act of 1975," recording of deeds and other real property transactions and inspection of public records, respectively, so as to provide for an unfair or deceptive practice in consumer transactions in the recording of certain residential real estate documents; to provide for related matters; to provide an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.changes: First version of the bill.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee's substitute pushes the key dates back one year. The state clerks' authority now has until January 1, 2027, instead of January 1, 2026, to adopt standards for remote online notarization. Applications to become a remote online notary also start January 1, 2027, instead of 2026. Apart from formatting changes, the rest of the bill is the same, including the rule that a licensed Georgia attorney must still supervise real estate closings.

bills.headline: Allows remote online notarization and electronic witnessing for Georgia real estate documents.
bills.recap: This bill creates a new class of remote online notaries who can notarize documents by live video, including deeds and other real estate documents, starting with state standards due by January 1, 2027. Notaries must take a course, pass an exam, carry a $2,000 bond, verify signer ID through set checks, keep a 10-year electronic journal and video recording, and may charge up to $25 per notarization. It also lets unofficial witnesses sign real estate documents electronically or by video, and tells clerks to record documents that show both witness signatures without digging further. The bill keeps the rule that a Georgia attorney must supervise closings and makes it an unfair business practice to knowingly record a 1-4 family home document that came from the unauthorized practice of law, which matters to agents working with remote or out-of-state buyers and sellers.

bills.title: Local government; procedures for real property owners to make claims for compensation for loss of property value or expenses incurred; provisions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 60 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to general provisions applicable to counties and municipal corporations, so as to provide procedures for real property owners to make claims for compensation from local governments for loss of property value or expenses incurred due to the local government's failure to comply with or nonenforcement of certain laws, ordinances, and resolutions or due to the local government maintaining a public nuisance; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version narrows when property owners can claim money from a city or county for lost property value or costs caused by non-enforcement of laws (like illegal camping or panhandling) or a public nuisance. It defines "policy, pattern, or practice" as a widespread, organized practice, so one-off or isolated failures do not count. It caps payments at the property taxes that local government collected over the prior two years, leaving out school taxes, and lets the government defend itself by showing it took reasonable steps to address the nuisance. It also makes an owner pay the government's legal fees if they keep filing after two unsuccessful claims on the same property, and it says claims are handled under an existing tax refund process (Code Section 48-5-380).

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The new substitute changes the claim deadline. Owners now must file within the same tax year the events happened, instead of within 24 months. It also changes the payment cap: compensation can't exceed the local property taxes paid on the parcel in the prior tax year, instead of the old cap tied to taxes from the two years before the claim. Owners whose claims are denied as incomplete may now revise and resubmit them. The penalty for repeat claims is tougher: after just one unsuccessful claim on a parcel (down from two), the local government recovers its legal fees and costs on any later failed claim. Repeat claims in later years now require ongoing money damages rather than just 'injury,' and the rest of the changes are wording cleanups and a new Code section number.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The only edit is to the header: the line naming the House Committee on Public Safety and Homeland Security as the source of the substitute was replaced with the bill number and a list of sponsors, including Representatives Gaines, Leverett, Crowe, Jones, and Anderson. The rules on how property owners can claim compensation for lost property value or expenses were not changed.

versions.name: Enrolled
versions.changes: The final version keeps the core plan: property owners can ask their city or county to pay them back for cleanup costs or lost property value caused by things like ignored illegal camping, panhandling, or immigration sanctuary policies, capped at the prior year's local property taxes. New sections let anyone harmed by a local sanctuary policy, or by a jail that ignores a federal immigration detainer, ask a superior court to order compliance, and those cases get priority. The rule making repeat losing claimants pay the local government's legal fees now applies only to claims that were complete when filed, so incomplete paperwork won't count against an owner. The bill title also mentions public disclosure of certain state documents, but no section in this version actually does that.

bills.headline: Lets property owners seek payment from local governments that ignore certain laws or nuisances.
bills.recap: This new law lets property owners and leaseholders file a written claim against their city or county if it has a policy or pattern of not enforcing laws on things like illegal camping, loitering, panhandling, public drug use, or shoplifting, of not following state immigration rules, or of maintaining a public nuisance. Owners can ask for either documented costs to deal with the problem or the drop in their property's fair market value, but payment is capped at the local property taxes paid on that parcel the prior year. If the local government rejects the claim or does not act within 30 days, the owner can sue, the government must prove its case, and a winning owner gets attorney fees. Realtors may see clients ask about this option when nearby conditions hurt home values, and claims are limited to once per tax year per parcel.

bills.title: Property; landlord and tenant; repeal Code Section 44-7-19, relating to restrictions on rent regulation by local governments
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, regarding landlord and tenant in general, so as to repeal Code Section 44-7-19, relating to restrictions on rent regulation by local governments; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

bills.headline: Repeals Georgia's ban on local governments regulating rents.
bills.recap: This bill repeals Code Section 44-7-19, the state law that restricts cities and counties from regulating rent. The bill itself does not create rent control. It removes the state-level barrier, which could let local governments adopt their own rent rules. Realtors who work with landlords, investors, or rental properties may want to watch this closely, since local rent rules could affect rental income and property values.

bills.title: Appeal and error; appeal of superior court decisions on zoning decisions of counties and municipal corporations; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 2 of Chapter 6 of Title 5 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to appellate practice, and Chapter 66 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to zoning procedures as pertaining to counties and municipal corporations, so as to provide for the appeal of superior court decisions on zoning decisions of counties and municipal corporations; to repeal provisions authorizing administrative officers to exercise zoning powers; to repeal provisions authorizing quasi-judicial boards and agencies to hear and render decisions on applications for special administrative permits and conditional permits; to revise definitions; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

bills.headline: Revises Georgia zoning procedures and lets superior court zoning rulings be appealed directly.
bills.recap: This bill lets final superior court rulings on local zoning decisions be appealed directly to Georgia's higher courts. It also changes zoning rules for cities and counties: it removes the power of staff officers to make quasi-judicial zoning calls, shortens hearing notice for boards like zoning appeals boards from 30 to 15 days, and requires those boards to adopt written decision standards. It treats special use permits as zoning decisions handled by elected officials and shortens the gap between the two votes needed to allow multifamily uses in single-family zones from 21 to 15 days. Realtors with clients seeking rezonings, variances, or special use permits may see changes in timelines, notice, and how disputes reach the courts.

bills.title: Revenue and taxation; tax credits for certain contributions made by taxpayers to certain mortgage loan originators; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 2 of Chapter 7 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to imposition, rate, computation, exemption, and credits, so as to provide for tax credits for certain contributions made by taxpayers to certain mortgage loan originators; to provide for definitions; to provide for an aggregate annual limit; to provide for terms and conditions; to provide for applications and certifications; to provide for the revocation of qualified status; to provide for certain penalties; to provide for the promulgation of rules and regulations; to provide for related matters; to provide for an effective date and applicability; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.changes: First version of the bill.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The House Ways and Means Committee version cuts the yearly statewide cap on these tax credits from $20 million to $10 million. It also lowers the credit limit for corporations and other entities from 75% to 30% of their state income tax bill, and drops the rule that let unused credits carry forward for five years, so unused credits are now lost. A new step lets the state approve leftover credits on a first-come, first-served basis from July 1 to December 31, but credits approved in that window are limited to 95% of the normal amount. Overall, the program for donations to exempt mortgage loan originators is smaller and less generous than in the original bill.

bills.headline: Creates state tax credits for donations to certain nonprofit-style exempt mortgage lenders.
bills.recap: This bill gives Georgia taxpayers a state income tax credit for preapproved donations to mortgage loan originators that are exempt from state licensing and certified by the Department of Revenue. Credits run from 2026 through 2030 and are capped at $10 million a year statewide, with each organization limited to $2 million a year. Individuals can claim up to $5,000, couples up to $10,000, and corporations up to 30% of their tax bill. The bill does not say how the money must be used, but it could mean more funding for exempt lenders that help buyers get mortgages.

bills.title: Bryan County; ad valorem tax; educational purposes; provide homestead exemption
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to provide a homestead exemption from Bryan County school district ad valorem taxes for educational purposes in an amount equal to the amount by which the current year assessed value of a homestead exceeds the adjusted base year assessed value of such homestead; to provide for definitions; to specify the terms and conditions of the exemption and the procedures relating thereto; to provide for applicability; to provide for compliance with constitutional requirements; to provide for a referendum, effective dates, automatic repeal, mandatory execution of election, and judicial remedies regarding failure to comply; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

bills.headline: Caps yearly school tax assessment increases on Bryan County homesteads at the inflation rate.
bills.recap: This bill creates a homestead exemption from Bryan County school district taxes that limits how much a home's taxable value can rise each year to the rate of inflation, plus any value from improvements. It covers up to five contiguous acres and starts January 1, 2026, if Bryan County school district voters approve it in a November 2025 referendum. Homeowners who already have a 2025 homestead exemption get it automatically, but the benefit does not transfer to a new owner. Realtors should know that buyers will be taxed on the home's current value, so their school taxes may be higher than what the seller paid.

bills.title: Local government; residential rental property; establish housing management databases
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 2 of Chapter 74 of Title 36 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to local enforcement boards created on or after January 1, 2003, so as to authorize local governing bodies to establish housing management databases of residential rental property; to provide for applicability; to provide for registration with the databases; to provide for penalties; to provide for disclosure of ownership by foreign adversaries; to provide for exemptions; to provide for definitions; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version narrows who can be required to join a local rental housing database. It now applies only to owners with at least ten connected (contiguous) units, up from five units anywhere in the area. It also leaves out homes licensed by the Department of Community Health, multifamily properties with more than 20 units, and short-term rentals. Owners can list either their own or their property manager's contact information. Property managers may also handle updates and the foreign ownership disclosure, and the list of foreign adversaries now follows the U.S. Commerce Department's list instead of naming specific countries.

bills.headline: Lets local governments require rental owners with 10+ contiguous units to register in databases.
bills.recap: This bill lets Georgia cities and counties create a free registry of residential rental property, but only for owners who own or control at least 10 contiguous units in that area. Properties with more than 20 units, certain state-licensed homes, and short-term rentals under 30 days are excluded. Owners or property managers would list contact details, the property address and parcel number, and deed information, update it within 30 days of changes, and disclose any foreign adversary ownership. Fines can run from $500 to $1,000 per violation, with exemptions for deployed military, serious illness, heirs, and disaster hardship. Notices of code violations could also go to the property manager, which matters for licensees who manage rentals.

bills.title: Property; prohibit homeowners' associations from preventing property owners from installing solar energy devices; provisions
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property, so as to prohibit condominium associations, property owners' associations, and homeowners' associations from preventing property owners from installing solar energy devices on common roofs or roof structures; to provide for the burden of costs for removal and reinstallation of solar energy devices; to allow for repair of common roofs or roof structures; to provide for definitions; to provide for applicability; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.name: Introduced
versions.changes: First version of the bill.

bills.headline: Bars HOAs and condo associations from blocking owners' rooftop solar installations.
bills.recap: This bill stops condo associations, property owners' associations, and HOAs from banning or restricting solar energy devices on an owner's roof, even when the roof is a common area the association maintains. Associations could not require a permit or charge a fee for installing or using solar, and any rule or covenant that conflicts would be void. If the roof needs maintenance later, the owner who installed the solar must pay to remove and reinstall it. The rules would apply to covenants, documents, and association rules made, renewed, or changed on or after January 1, 2026, which matters for agents advising buyers and sellers in HOA and condo communities.

bills.title: Property; require certain residential landlords to have in-state staff to manage tenant communications
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Article 1 of Chapter 7 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to landlords and tenants in general, so as to require certain residential landlords to have in-state staff to manage tenant communications related to such properties; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.changes: First version of the bill.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The committee version adds a new requirement for landlords who own or operate 25 or more single-family or duplex rentals in Georgia. They must now employ a Georgia-licensed real estate broker, who does not have to live in Georgia. The rule from the original bill stays: these landlords must still employ at least one person located in Georgia to receive and respond to tenant maintenance and other property issues. This could create more demand for licensed brokers among large single-family rental owners.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The new version narrows who the rule covers. It now applies only to landlords who are not Georgia residents and own or operate 25 or more single-family or duplex rentals in the state. Before, it applied to any landlord with that many properties. Those covered landlords must still hire a licensed broker, who can live in or out of state, plus at least one person located in Georgia to handle tenant maintenance and other calls.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: Nothing meaningful changed in this version. The header now lists the bill's sponsors (Representatives Oliver, Olaleye, Burnough, Blackmon, Frye, and others) instead of naming the House Governmental Affairs Committee. The only other edit is a spacing difference in one line of text. The bill's rules on landlords needing in-state staff for tenant communications are unchanged.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The Senate committee version drops the 25-property threshold, so any out-of-state landlord who owns or runs single-family or duplex rentals in Georgia must hire a Georgia-licensed broker. If that broker lives outside Georgia, the broker (not the landlord) must keep at least one in-state person to handle tenant maintenance calls and other issues. These landlords also can no longer use the owner and full-time-employee exemptions from real estate licensing, and the owner exemption now covers management company owners whose principals hold controlling ownership of the property. A new rule also says that when a code officer has probable cause of a violation at a broker-managed rental, the tenant must, on request, give the property manager's name, license number, and contact information.

versions.name: Comm Sub
versions.changes: The one real change adds family members of an owner to the list of people who can manage or lease the owner's property without a real estate license. The Georgia Real Estate Commission would define who counts as a family member in its rules. Before, the exemption covered only the owner, the owner's spouse, and certain others. bills.headline: Out-of-state landlords of single-family homes and duplexes must hire a Georgia-licensed broker.
bills.recap: Landlords who live outside Georgia and own or operate single-family or duplex rentals here must hire a broker licensed in Georgia. If that broker lives out of state, the broker must have at least one person in Georgia to handle tenant calls about repairs and other issues. These landlords can no longer use the owner and full-time employee exemptions to skip licensing. The bill also lets code enforcement officers, when they have probable cause of a violation, ask tenants for the property manager's name, license number, and contact info. For Realtors, this could create new property management business and adds accountability for licensed managers.

bills.title: Community Housing Options Increase Cost Efficiency (CHOICE) Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Titles 12, 32, and 50 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to conservation and natural resources, highways, bridges, and ferries, and state government, respectively, so as to provide for a system whereby certain local governments may seek certifications from the Department of Community Affairs upon the enactment of certain policies that can be used to receive priority in grant and loan applications submitted to state agencies; to provide for statutory construction; to provide that the Georgia Environmental Finance Authority give priority to certified local governments when awarding grants and loans; to provide definitions; to provide exceptions; to provide for related matters; to provide a short title; to provide legislative findings; to provide an effective date; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

The law would now take effect July 1, 2026 instead of July 1, 2025. Local governments could start applying for housing certifications from the Department of Community Affairs on July 1, 2027 instead of 2026. The department would start publishing yearly income data on January 1, 2027 instead of 2026. The housing policies, certification levels, and grant and loan priority rules are unchanged.

bills.headline: Rewards local governments with grant priority for adopting zoning reforms that boost housing supply.
bills.recap: The CHOICE Act lets larger or higher-income Georgia cities and counties earn a state certification starting July 1, 2027, by adopting a set number of pro-housing policies. Examples include allowing duplexes, ADUs, townhomes, and cottage courtyards in single-family zones, smaller minimum home sizes and lot sizes, reduced parking and setbacks, faster permits, and not requiring HOAs for new developments. Certified communities would get priority for certain state grants and loans from DCA, GEFA, and the recreational trails program, and top-tier ones would not need matching funds for some road grants. Participation is voluntary, but Realtors could see more housing types, more building, and new development options in communities that sign on.

bills.headline: Limits HOA liens, bans big REIT home buys, allows local rent control, curbs foreclosures.
bills.recap: This bill removes the automatic lien that condo and property owners' associations get for unpaid fees, which also removes their power to foreclose over those debts, though owners would still owe the money. It voids any sale of a single-family home or townhome to a real estate investment trust that already owns at least $30 million or 12,000 units of rental homes in Georgia. It repeals the state ban on local rent control and blocks non-court (power of sale) foreclosures against borrowers who are 65 or older or under guardianship, for loans made or changed after the law takes effect. Realtors should watch this closely: it could change HOA payoff letters at closing, cut off a major group of buyers, and change how foreclosures and rental markets work.

bills.title: Homeowners Protection Act; enact
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to property, so as to enact the "Homeowners Protection Act"; to provide for a rental intention affidavit regarding dispossessory proceedings; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

bills.headline: Lets owners file an affidavit to speed removal of squatters from their property.
bills.recap: This bill creates the "Homeowners Protection Act." It lets a property owner file a sworn statement with the county superior court clerk saying the property is not rented and asking that any unlawful occupant be removed within one calendar day once the statement is confirmed. That statement can then be used as the basis to demand possession in an eviction (dispossessory) case. Realtors may care because it gives owners of vacant homes, listings, and investment properties a faster tool against squatters.

bills.title: Ad valorem tax; additional period to appeal certain property assessments; provide
bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 5 of Title 48 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to ad valorem taxation of property, so as to provide for an additional period to appeal certain property assessments; to require the annual notice of assessment for property taxes to include an estimate of the current year's taxes and a statement regarding such estimate; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

bills.headline: Gives property owners a second chance to appeal assessments after receiving their tax bill.
bills.recap: This bill lets property owners appeal their assessed value within 45 days of the assessment notice or within 30 days of getting their actual tax bill. It also requires the yearly assessment notice to include an estimate of the current year's taxes, based on the prior or most applicable millage rate, along with a bold statement that the real bill may differ and may not include all exemptions. Forest land conservation use applications would follow the same appeal deadlines. Realtors may care because owners and recent buyers get more time to challenge high valuations and clearer early estimates of their tax costs.

bills.recap: This local bill creates a homestead exemption from Bryan County school district taxes. It covers up to five acres and starts January 1, 2026, but only if Bryan County school district voters approve it in a November 2025 referendum. Current homestead owners get it automatically, but it does not carry over to a new owner, so buyers should expect the school tax bill to reset after a sale.

bills.description: A BILL to be entitled an Act to amend Chapter 3 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated, relating to regulation of specialized land transactions, so as to prohibit business enterprises from owning an interest in more than 2,000 single-family residential properties or ten multifamily residential properties; to provide for the forfeiture of rental payments paid in connection with an unlawful lease of residential property; to provide a private cause of action for the return of rental payments paid in connection with an unlawful lease of residential property; to provide for the disclosure of information by brokers; to provide an effective date; to provide a short title; to provide for related matters; to repeal conflicting laws; and for other purposes.

versions.changes: The House Judiciary Committee's version makes a few targeted changes; most of the bill is unchanged. Condos now count as single-family residences, so they fall under the 2,000-home cap on business ownership. The meaning of 'business enterprise' now names 'issuers' as covered, and only an 'aggrieved' person can sue. The bill now says each home held over the limit by a business or one of its shareholders counts as a separate violation. The $15,000-per-violation damages, forced public sale, lease limits, and the rule that brokers must tell business clients about these limits all stay the same.

bills.headline: Caps business ownership at 2,000 single-family homes or ten multifamily properties in Georgia.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2026, this bill would make it illegal for a business, counting its affiliates, to own more than 2,000 single-family homes (including townhouses and condos) or more than ten apartment properties with four or more units in Georgia. Anyone harmed could sue for actual damages or $15,000 per property, plus attorney's fees. The Attorney General or a district attorney could force a public sale of homes held over the limit, and businesses over the cap could not lease those homes; tenants could sue to get their rent back but keep their leases. Brokers working with business clients buying or leasing out homes must tell them about these limits, so it adds a new disclosure duty for agents and could shift investor demand in many markets.

Any Section 179 amount already taken on single-family rentals would have to be added back to Georgia taxable income. The change applies to corporations, and the bill text also changes the rules for individual taxpayers. Realtors who work with investors buying single-family rentals may see clients face higher state tax bills, which could affect how attractive these purchases look.

versions.changes: The Senate Judiciary substitute narrows the flood disclosure rule to arm's-length sales of one-to-four family homes, and only to floods during the current seller's ownership. Sellers must affirm or deny each item. The floodplain and erosion items were dropped, and only dates of floods and the nature of repairs must be listed, not repair costs. Only a willful failure to disclose now violates the Fair Business Practices Act, and the rule that flood damage is automatically an adverse material fact was removed. The bill also says sellers and brokers do not have to investigate. It adds a $1,500-per-lien fine, plus attorney's fees or court costs, for mechanic's liens filed in bad faith or without good reason. It now takes effect January 1, 2026, instead of when signed.

versions.changes: This new Senate Judiciary Committee version pushes the start date back one year, from January 1, 2026 to January 1, 2027. The rest of the changes are just updated document labels. bills.headline: Requires home sellers to disclose flood damage, claims, and repairs; fines frivolous mechanic liens.
bills.recap: Starting January 1, 2027, sellers of one-to-four family homes in Georgia must give buyers a written statement confirming or denying any flood damage, flood insurance claims, flood repairs, repetitive loss notices, or federal flood insurance requirements during their ownership, including approximate flood dates and the type of repairs. A willful failure to disclose counts as a violation of the Fair Business Practices Act. Sellers and their agents do not have to investigate beyond what the seller already knows. The bill also sets a $1,500 fine per lien, plus attorney's fees or court costs, for mechanic liens filed without good faith or with malice.

bills.headline: Creates a Georgia civil rights law and adds sexual orientation and age to fair housing protections.
bills.recap: HB670 would create the Georgia Civil Rights Act of 2025, banning discrimination in housing, public places, and jobs based on race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, age, disability, familial status, or national origin. For real estate, it adds sexual orientation and age to the Georgia Fair Housing Act. That covers sales, rentals, lending, advertising, appraisals, and access to MLS and Realtor organizations. Agents, brokers, landlords, lenders, and appraisers would need to update their practices and ads to follow the wider rules, which would take effect January 1, 2026.

bills.headline: Bans landlords from using shared data or software to coordinate rental prices.
bills.recap: This bill makes it illegal for competing landlords to agree to set rents using shared rental data run through pricing software, including AI tools. Such agreements would be void, and anyone who enters into one could face a felony with 1 to 5 years in prison, fines of $1,000 to $5,000, or both. Landlords also could not set rents based on that kind of pooled-data pricing. The rules cover owners and their agents, including property managers. Work done under affordable or low-income housing programs is exempt. Realtors who manage rentals or advise investors should watch how this could change the pricing tools they use.

This bill removes that local option. It says neither the state code nor any local code adopted after May 24, 2010 may require sprinklers in single-family homes or duplexes. Realtors may care because sprinkler mandates can raise the cost of building new homes, so this could help keep new construction prices down.

bills.headline: Caps yearly rent increases for seniors and veterans living mainly on federal benefits.
bills.recap: This bill limits how much a landlord can raise rent in a 12-month period when renewing or re-signing a lease with an existing tenant who is 62 or older, or a veteran, and whose main income is Social Security or veterans' benefits. The cap is the lower of 5% plus the yearly change in the Consumer Price Index, or 10%, measured against the lowest rent charged in the past 12 months. Rent includes most fees, but not security deposits. If a landlord charges more than allowed, the tenant can use that as a defense and counterclaim in an eviction case. The rule would apply to leases signed or renewed on or after July 1, 2025, and would end on January 1, 2035. Property managers and leasing agents would need to track tenant eligibility and limit renewal increases.

bills.recap: If a landlord does not respond to a needed repair within five days, the tenant could hire a licensed professional and take the cost out of rent, capped at 50 percent of any one payment and backed by receipts. The bill also gives tenants 14 days instead of 7 to answer an eviction notice or pay back rent to stop the case. It also delays writs of possession to 14 days after judgment instead of 7. It would apply to residential leases signed or renewed on or after July 1, 2025, so agents who manage property or represent investors should watch it closely.

bills.headline: Caps residential rent increases at 3 percent yearly and requires 120 days' notice.
bills.recap: This bill would limit rent increases on most Georgia homes and apartments to 3 percent over the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months, with 120 days' notice required, and no increases mid-lease unless the lease allows it. Rent hikes for qualifying students and seniors would be capped at 2 percent, and some low-income seniors renting the same place over five years could freeze their rent for up to five years. Buildings built after 2024 are exempt for 15 years, as are government-subsidized and state college housing. Violations would count as unfair trade practices, and tenants could use overcharges as a defense in evictions, so landlords, property managers, and investor clients would face new limits.

Fees like stormwater, trash, water and sewer charges, plus late fees or interest on those items, must be billed separately. Costs tied to collecting late property taxes can still appear on the tax bill. It would apply to bills issued on or after January 1, 2026, and could change how agents explain annual tax costs, escrow amounts, and closing prorations to clients.

bills.recap: This bill adds AI and automated decision tools to Georgia's fair housing law, so discrimination caused by these tools counts as illegal discrimination. Relying on AI is not a defense against a discrimination claim. Anyone using AI for decisions about selling, renting, financing, or brokerage services for homes must have a person review those decisions and must tell affected people that AI was used. The Attorney General could fine violators up to $10,000, so agents, brokers, landlords, and lenders using AI screening or pricing tools should take note.

bills.recap: This bill expands Georgia's basic landlord repair duty into a detailed list of minimum living standards. Rentals would need to be structurally sound, with safe water, working heat and cooling, ventilation, lighting, safe electrical service, sanitary bathrooms and kitchens, and a second way out in case of fire. Each occupied level would need a working smoke detector, with special alarms for hearing-impaired tenants, and common areas like laundry rooms and hallways would also need detectors. Realtors who work with investors, property managers, or renters should know these standards could raise compliance costs for landlords and give tenants clearer grounds to demand repairs.

Voters must approve both the sales tax and a matching local homestead exemption, and the deal ends after 10 years unless renewed. For Realtors, it could noticeably lower property tax bills for owner-occupants, which may affect affordability and how homes are marketed.

bills.recap: This bill requires landlords or managers of apartment buildings and complexes to give local police and fire departments current after-hours maintenance and management phone numbers.
